explanations.explanation: It appears that the feature is sensitive to common morphological suffixes—those short subword endings (like “thens,” “ious,” “ings,” “get,” “ine,” “form,” “ally,” “ancy,” “ed,” etc.) that modify a word’s meaning. In other words, it detects derivational inflections that change a stem into an adjective, noun, or similar form, and this in turn strongly influences the model’s subsequent token prediction.

It appears that the feature “flags” a present‐or “recent” announcement or status update—i.e. a temporal framing marker that sets a current, live or news‐style context. This token pattern biases the model toward continuations (like a comma or “for”) that fit an immediate, update‐oriented register.

This feature appears to mark points where the text shifts into an explanatory or goal‐directed clause—a “discourse transition” signal that cues the model to generate a subordinate, often causal or purpose‐driven continuation (e.g. “for this reason”, an infinitive “to” clause, or a key “deal”) rather than a generic follow‐on like “tell” or “date.”

It signals a “fill‐in” or instructional input context—a syntactic and semantic marker that occurs in directive, form‐filling texts. Its presence “primes” the pattern (e.g. “fill in the …”) so that the following token is the expected article in an instruction, whereas without it the continuation shifts toward a different construction.

It appears the model has “learned” an abstract morpheme‐pattern—a latent subword feature that flags a stem whose inflection or derivation is about to be completed (e.g. “protect” → “protection”, “elect” → “electronic”, “rapid” → “rapidly”, “surviv” → “survivors”, etc.). In other words, this feature signals that a particular word‐root is in play and primes the model to continue with a predictable, derivational suffix.

The feature seems to trigger when the text is addressing or requesting a definition or explanation—that is, it detects moments when “meaning” (or its variants, embedded in words like “mean,” “means,” “ends,” etc.) is being invoked to pose or introduce an interpretive inquiry.

It appears that the feature is a sort of sentence‐boundary detector—a signal activated by end‐of‐sentence punctuation (often a period) that conditions the model to treat the following token in a boundary‐sensitive way (altering what comes next, such as capitalization or phrase shifts).

It appears to be a feature that “lights up” when the model is framing a direct, evaluative question—typically one beginning with “What” (and similar wh-phrases) that asks for a qualitative, comparative, or opinion-based response.

It detects sentences’ introductory or subordinate “context‐setter” phrases (often starting with “Having,” “But,” “While,” etc.) that signal background or qualifying context in narrative discourse, thereby influencing how the model continues the text.

This feature appears to detect the “end‐marker” of a formal or named entity—a punctuation or token fragment that signals a complete, structured label (such as a corporate name, institution, or branded term). Its activation cues the model to continue with entity‐specific completions rather than a generic word continuation.

explanations.explanation: It appears that the feature is sensitive to a “comparison cue” – a short string (often resembling parts of adverbs or simile markers like “ally,” “ost,” “other,” or “like”) that signals a comparative or analogical construction. In other words, when these substrings appear, the model is biased toward completing a simile or comparison phrase.

This feature encodes a discrete sentence‐ or phrase–boundary signal—essentially a learned punctuation separator—that cues the model to “close off” one segment before the next begins. When the feature is removed, the model instead predicts leftover suffix fragments (like “ces” or “ages”), indicating that the proper punctuation‐boundary signal is absent.

It appears that the feature is a latent signal for “completing” a lexical unit – a sort of built‐in segmentation or word‐boundary marker. In other words, when the model “sees” this signal (often on the tail end of a name, compound, or split word), it treats the token as a completed unit and shifts its next token expectations (for example, toward a proper follow‐up word rather than a punctuation mark). This feature thereby encodes an abstract notion of morphological or entity‐boundary completion that guides the syntactic and semantic flow of the text.

It appears this feature “lights‐up” when the model is in a complaint/evaluation mode—that is, when a word (like “trouble,” “questions,” “strange,” “fantastic,” etc.) signals a problematic or opinionated situation, the model shifts its next‐token expectations (for example, preferring a complement like “with” rather than the default “to”). In short, the feature encodes a kind of evaluative or issue‐reporting idiom that biases the continuation toward the appropriate syntactic/semantic frame for describing problems or judgments.

It appears that this feature encodes a positive, celebratory sentiment—a kind of pride/affect signal—that shows up in contexts where the speaker emphasizes valued experiences or achievements and shapes upcoming syntactic choices (for example, favoring an infinitive “to” construction over alternatives).

It’s a feature that flags when a capital-letter abbreviation (an initial) is followed by its period—a punctuation signal that the token is part of a proper‐name abbreviation—which in turn affects the model’s expectation for the following token.

It reliably signals that a token is functioning not as a stand‐alone word (often a common linking word like “of”) but as an internal piece of a compound or affixed unit—i.e. a marker of nonstandard subword segmentation (such as in hyphenated words, unit abbreviations, or clitic endings) that alters the model’s next‐token expectations.

It’s a punctuation‐boundary detector—specifically, a feature sensitive to sentence‑ending periods that signals a transition to a new sentence (often altering capitalization or ensuing proper‑noun contexts), thereby guiding the model’s next token predictions.

It appears this feature activates on tokens that signal abbreviated proper names – a brief (often single‐letter) entity or title marker ending in a period used as a middle initial or other shorthand (e.g. “M.”, “ST.”, “G.”, “St.”). In context, the model reliably flags these abbreviated name components that set off or introduce proper noun sequences.

It signals a sentence‐ or segment–boundary marker – the model is detecting periods that mark the end of structured, factual snippets (such as dates, prices, or event headlines), cueing a break between information units.

It’s a signal for a sentence‐ or clause‐boundary marker—especially when an abbreviation or title (like “Gov.”) immediately precedes strong punctuation—which cues the model to switch contexts (affecting the next token prediction).

explanations.explanation: This feature seems to be a signal for contexts where a terminal (or abbreviation‐ending) punctuation is meant to indicate that the following token should be “reset” into a new, typically proper‐noun or sentence–initial style. In other words, it cues the model that the punctuation marks the end of a clause or an abbreviation—shifting the next token’s distribution from a generic default like “December” or “Need” to one appropriate for names/initials (e.g. “Louis”, “I”, “J”).

It appears that this feature is a detector for sentence‐boundary punctuation—especially the period that ends a sentence or an abbreviation like “Gov.”—which signals a context and style shift in generation (often priming the next sentence start with a token like “This”).

It appears to be a subword‐ or morpheme–boundary signal—that is, a feature that lights up on “continuation pieces” (affixes or other split fragments within a word) that cue the model to treat that subword chunk as having a distinct, context‐modifying role in how the upcoming token is predicted.

It appears that this feature “fires” on periods used as sentence‐end markers in contexts where a decisively “ended” thought is signaled. In practical terms, it prevents the model from defaulting to a common domain suffix (“.com”) when a sentence really should stop rather than continue as a website. This feature thus encodes the distinction between a true sentence‐end period and a period that might otherwise trigger URL‐like continuations.

It appears that this feature is “noticing” a morphological sub‐unit—a key suffix or segment inside a compound or technical term—that signals a particular semantic or functional class. In other words, it activates on the part of a word that, when present, cues the model to treat the term as a specialized term (for instance, an agent or descriptor in chemical, biological, or technical language), thereby shifting the next‐token prediction accordingly.

It appears that this feature “lights up” on sentence‐initiating interrogative (or statement–introductory) tokens—especially words like “What” (and in one case “True”)—and it encourages the network to “uncontract” the following auxiliary (predicting “is” or a punctuation) rather than tacking on a clitic “s.” In short, the feature encodes that the token is the head of an interrogative (or declarative) clause, steering the model toward the proper expansion of the subsequent function word instead of a contracted form.

It’s a feature that “steers” the model away from its default, over‐generalized “-ation” ending by detecting and favoring the correct, irregular or morphologically appropriate word‐end segments (e.g. “ide,” “rot,” “iding,” “ate,” “less,” “ome”) so that the full word is completed correctly rather than with the common suffix.
